Caesar wrote about these battles, including the conquest of Lutetia, which he described as being situated on an island in the Seine River. Archaeologists conducting excavations near Notre-Dame Cathedral recently uncovered centuries of French history, including evidence of the city’s Roman occupation after Caesar’s conquest of Lutetia.

Some scholars thought it might have been in the heart of Paris, or perhaps near the western suburb of Nanterre, based on archaeological discoveries made there in the 1990s.

Researchers hope to continue excavating at the site, but the work will be limited to areas undergoing renovations, so progress might be slow. Because the wall is too fragile to be preserved, archaeologists will construct a mold in order to create a replica that can incorporate original stones and eventually be displayed in a Paris museum. Researchers also plan to develop a 3D digital model for members of the public to explore.

“All of our predecessors dreamed of finding traces of Gallic presences on the Île de la Cité,” Dorothée Chaoui-Derieux, who coordinates archaeological operations in Paris for France’s Ministry of Culture, tells the AFP. “There has been a lot of speculation on the subject. We’re fortunate to be in the right place at the right time.”

Archaeologists in Paris have discovered the remains of an ancient wall that may have formed part of the city’s original settlement.

The Roman Empire conquered Lutetia in 52 B.C.E. during Julius Caesar’s eight-year campaign against the Gauls, a group of Celtic farmers who lived across what is now France, Belgium, Germany and Italy.

Archaeologists conducting excavations near Notre-Dame Cathedral recently uncovered centuries of French history, including evidence of the city’s Roman occupation after Caesar’s conquest of Lutetia.
